     * `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"` (quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without quasi-experimental intervention comparator)

     * `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"` (legal-empirical, doctrinal-empirical, jurimetric, or institutional-historical study that fits none of the six conventional designs above)
     * `"NONE"` (fits none of the listed tools, e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model, or non-systematic narrative review/essay without primary empirical data or systematic search — explain why in `comment`)

(`"2"` = mechanism directly observed empirically; `"1"` = documented statistical/descriptive association; `"0"` = inferred only by authors).

country.comment: Section 2.1 (PDF p. 4) states that the developing-country sample comprises 31 low-income countries (Table A1), 51 lower-middle-income countries (Table A2), and 53 higher-middle-income countries (Table A3), totaling 135 countries (note: Table A2 on PDF p. 18 prints 50 economies, making 134 listed across Tables A1-A3).
country.value: Global (135 low- and middle-income countries: 31 low-income, 51 lower-middle-income, 53 higher-middle-income)
country.where_found: PDF p. 4, Section 2.1; PDF pp. 18-19, Appendix A, Tables A1-A3

effect_estimate.comment: Headline empirical findings come from country-year fixed-effects Prais-Winsten GLS regressions (Tables 2-7). Both governance-indicator associations and socioeconomic correlates are reported with exact printed coefficients, robust standard errors, significance thresholds, and country-year observation counts (N). Note that Table 6 prints Weak Regulatory 1.639*** with (0.504) on the next row due to a table-formatting shift on PDF p. 16, and Table 7 similarly shifts standard errors on the Weak/Very weak Regulatory rows on PDF p. 17.
effect_estimate.value: In global country-year fixed-effects Prais-Winsten GLS regressions of rural water access (%) across developing countries: (1) Governance indicators: For rural piped water on premises (Table 3, N = 1,691 / 1,076 / 1,573), Weak Regulatory Quality is negatively associated with piped access in the female-education specification (beta = -2.252, SE = 0.834, p < 0.01, N = 1,076) and agriculture specification (beta = -1.809, SE = 0.564, p < 0.01, N = 1,573; Very weak Regulatory beta = -1.469, SE = 0.778, p < 0.10), though null in the LogGNI specification (beta = 0.126, SE = 0.362, N = 1,691); Very weak Government Effectiveness reduces piped access (beta = -1.438, SE = 0.588, p < 0.05 in LogGNI model; beta = -9.874, SE = 2.494, p < 0.01 in Female model), as do Weak and Very weak Voice and Accountability in the Female model (beta = -2.429, SE = 0.591, p < 0.01; beta = -3.397, SE = 1.402, p < 0.05). For total improved rural water access (Table 2, N = 1,713 / 1,087 / 1,593), Weak Rule of Law consistently reduces access across all three global specifications (beta = -2.272, SE = 0.312, p < 0.01; beta = -1.637, SE = 0.614, p < 0.01; beta = -1.078, SE = 0.358, p < 0.01), alongside Weak Voice and Accountability (beta = -0.631, p < 0.05; -2.024, p < 0.01; -0.982, p < 0.01) and Weak Political Stability (beta = -0.621, p < 0.01; -0.838, p < 0.01; -0.381, p < 0.05). Conversely, for non-piped other improved rural water sources (Table 4, N = 1,697 / 1,083 / 1,577), Weak Regulatory Quality is positively associated with access across all three global specifications (beta = 2.017, SE = 0.635, p < 0.01; beta = 2.943, SE = 0.915, p < 0.01; beta = 3.368, SE = 0.763, p < 0.01). (2) Income-group subsamples (Tables 5-7): In middle-high income countries (Table 5, N = 343-351), Weak Rule of Law reduces total improved (beta = -0.977, SE = 0.490, p < 0.05) and piped access (beta = -1.707, SE = 0.658, p < 0.01), while Weak Regulatory Quality increases other improved access (beta = 3.955, SE = 1.074, p < 0.01). In middle-low income countries (Table 6, N = 408-458), Weak and Very weak Government Effectiveness reduce piped access (beta = -1.123, SE = 0.567, p < 0.05; beta = -2.863, SE = 0.750, p < 0.01) and Very weak Voice reduces total improved access (beta = -9.386, SE = 2.059, p < 0.01). In low-income countries (Table 7, N = 260-294), governance indicators are largely non-robust (Very weak Regulatory beta = -0.636, SE = 0.305, p < 0.05 and Weak Effectiveness beta = 0.486, SE = 0.199, p < 0.05 for piped access). (3) Socioeconomic and aid correlates (Global, Tables 2-4): LogGNI increases total improved (beta = 10.583, SE = 0.425, p < 0.01) and piped access (beta = 11.034, SE = 0.563, p < 0.01) while reducing other improved access (beta = -2.975, SE = 0.454, p < 0.01); lagged female primary completion rate increases total improved (beta = 0.234, SE = 0.020, p < 0.01) and piped access (beta = 0.154, SE = 0.024, p < 0.01); agriculture (% GDP) reduces total improved (beta = -0.391, SE = 0.026, p < 0.01) and piped access (beta = -0.409, SE = 0.032, p < 0.01); and lagged water/sanitation ODA (% GDP) is null for total improved and negative for piped access (beta = -2.654, p < 0.10; -8.421, p < 0.05; -6.519, p < 0.01).

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 1 (Documented association): the study estimates macro-level statistical associations between national World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators (Rule of Law, Voice and Accountability, Political Stability, Control of Corruption, Government Effectiveness, Regulatory Quality) and rural water access percentages, without directly observing specific legal or administrative mechanisms in operation (e.g., the authors explicitly hypothesize on PDF p. 14 that weaker regulatory regimes may ease informal/communal or private-well water provision, and on PDF pp. 8 and 11 that educated women may exert community pressure for water projects). Strictly obeys the <= 2 ceiling for non-experimental/non-ROBINS-I observational regressions.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 8-10, Section 2.4; PDF pp. 10-17, Section 3.1-3.4, Tables 2-7

mechanism_flags.comment: The study does not examine household-level legal eligibility or connection-application rules, but empirically tests national governance indicators (PDF pp. 9-10) defined as 'rules, enforcement mechanisms, and organizations'—specifically WGI Rule of Law (compliance with rules, contracts, property rights, police, and courts), Regulatory Quality (stringency of government regulations over private/communal water providers), Control of Corruption, and Government Effectiveness (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, ENFORCEMENT)—as well as citizen participation via WGI Voice and Accountability and women's education as a proxy for community participation in rural water project decision-making (participation).
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 8-10, Section 2.4; PDF pp. 13-17, Section 3.1-3.4

outcome_flags.comment: Section 2.3 (PDF p. 6) defines three national rural water coverage dependent variables from WHO/UNICEF JMP data: 'total improved' (proportion of rural population with access to improved water sources), 'piped on premises' (proportion of rural population with piped household water connections located inside the user's dwelling, plot, or yard), and 'other improved' (proportion of rural population using non-piped improved sources). Sanitation access, water quality, reliability, and affordability are discussed as background only and not analyzed as outcomes.
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF p. 6, Section 2.3; PDF pp. 11-17, Tables 2-7

publication_year.comment: Explicitly printed in the article publication history, running header/footer, and copyright line.
publication_year.where_found: PDF p. 1, article header and footer; PDF p. 21, copyright notice

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Observational macro-panel regression of socioeconomic and governance correlates across countries without a specific policy/intervention or quasi-experimental comparator (hence not ROBINS-I, which requires evaluating a specific policy/intervention with a comparator, and not an exposed/unexposed cohort study of baseline-outcome-free subjects, though longitudinal at the country-year panel level). Mapped to JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1 ('observational survey or regression without quasi-experimental intervention comparator').
risk_of_bias_tool.value: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

sample_size.comment: Unbalanced country-year panel covering up to 135 developing countries over 1990-2015 (with ODA measured over 1995-2015, reducing regression observation counts depending on covariate availability). Exact country-year observation counts (N) are printed at the bottom of each regression column in Tables 2-7.
sample_size.value: 135 developing countries (31 low-income, 51 lower-middle-income, 53 higher-middle-income as stated in text; 134 listed in Tables A1-A3) over 1990-2015 (ODA 1995-2015); global regressions N = 1,713, 1,087, and 1,593 country-year observations (Total improved), N = 1,691, 1,076, and 1,573 (Piped), and N = 1,697, 1,083, and 1,577 (Other improved); subgroup regressions N = 343-351 (middle-high income), N = 408-458 (middle-low income), and N = 260-294 (low income)
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 3, Section 1; PDF p. 4, Section 2.1; PDF p. 9, Section 2.4; PDF pp. 11-17, Tables 2-7; PDF pp. 18-19, Tables A1-A3

study_design.comment: Longitudinal macro-econometric country-year panel fixed-effects design without a specific intervention/comparator, using Stata 13 'xtpcse' (Prais-Winsten GLS) with country and year dummy variables, 1-year lags on female primary completion rate and ODA, and separate specifications/subsamples by World Bank income group.
study_design.value: Observational country-level panel data econometric study using two-way (country and year) linear fixed-effects regressions estimated via Prais-Winsten generalized least squares (GLS) with panel-corrected standard errors for heteroskedasticity and panel-specific AR(1) autocorrelation (1990-2015)
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 3, Section 1; PDF pp. 5-6, Section 2.2
